subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: planning fallacy from optimistic guessing [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. The manager asked how long the checkout module would take. Urmila wanted to please, and pictured everything going smoothly. "Six days," she said. No time for testing, none for reviews. Zainab looked up from the next desk but said nothing.

Day 5. The code review sat in a queue for two days, and the test environment crashed and took another day to repair.

Day 9. Zainab began her planned leave, and her part, a payment helper, had not been handed over.

Day 19. The module was finally delivered, thirteen days after the promise. The manager, who had told the client "Friday", had to write an apology.

qa.q: How many days did Urmila promise for the module?
What did Urmila want when giving the estimate?
qa.a: Urmila wanted to please the manager, and pictured everything going smoothly.

qa.q: What could Urmila do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Urmila could estimate each piece separately and add time for testing, reviews and colleagues' leave, because the best-case picture leaves no room for the usual delays.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt when writing the apology to the client?
qa.a: The manager probably felt embarrassed and let down, having promised the client a Friday on an estimate that had no slack.

grounding: Illustrates a developer wanting to please and giving a best-case estimate with no testing time, so reviews, environment problems and leave push delivery past the promise.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: planning fallacy from optimistic guessing [Pitfall]
passage:
"Elizabeth, you asked why I pad my estimates now. Here's the story. I'm Siddharth, and at twenty-four I was the most optimistic developer in Chennai.
My manager asked how long a new invoice feature would take. I wanted to impress her. I imagined everything going perfectly: no bugs, no waiting, no surprises. 'Five days,' I said. I didn't include testing. I didn't include reviews.
Day three, the test server went down for a day and a half. Day five, my code review came back with twelve comments. Day six, Kavya, the only person who understood the tax module, went on leave for a week.
It was delivered on day fifteen. Three times my promise.
My manager wasn't angry, just tired. She said, 'I planned the client call around your five days.' That hurt more than shouting.
So now I estimate the real version, not the dream."

qa.q: On which day was the invoice feature delivered?
qa.a: It was delivered on day fifteen.

qa.q: Why did young Siddharth give such a short estimate, and how did Siddharth feel?
qa.a: Siddharth was hopeful and eager to impress, imagining everything going perfectly.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Siddharth's story, and what should have been different?
qa.a: Estimating from the best case with no testing time was the key mistake; including reviews, testing and possible delays would have made the promise realistic.

qa.q: How did the manager feel about the late delivery?
qa.a: The manager felt tired and let down, having planned a client call around the five days.

grounding: Shows a developer, wanting to please, estimating from the best case with no testing time and delivering three times late after reviews, outages and leave.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: planning fallacy from optimistic guessing [Pitfall]
passage:
Varun's manager needed a new booking screen before the travel season, and asked on a Monday how long it would take. Varun, three years into his career and keen to make a good impression, did a quick sum in his head: design two days, code three. "One week," he said, smiling. He didn't mention testing.
His teammate Ujjwal raised an eyebrow. "Including reviews?"
"It'll be fine."
Wednesday, the office network went down for most of the day. Thursday, his code review came back with a long list of changes. The following Monday, Ujjwal, who was supposed to test it, left for his sister's wedding for five days.
The screen finally went live eighteen days after Varun's promise, just as the travel rush began. The manager had already told the sales team it was ready.
Varun sat at his desk late that night, staring at the "one week" message in his sent folder.

qa.q: How long after Varun's promise did the screen go live?
qa.a: It went live eighteen days after his promise.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he gave the one-week estimate?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and eager to impress, confident that everything would go smoothly.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Varun estimated?
qa.a: I would include testing, reviews and time for surprises like leave or outages, because the best case almost never happens.

qa.q: How might the sales team have been affected?
qa.a: The sales team had been told the screen was ready, so they likely felt embarrassed or frustrated in front of customers during the rush.

grounding: Shows a developer giving a best-case estimate with no testing time and then missing it badly after network issues, reviews and a colleague's leave.
